introduction-the-security-layers.core: Kubernetes security is layered: authentication (who), authorisation via RBAC (what), admission policies including Pod Security Standards (which objects are allowed), runtime security (seccomp, capabilities, sandboxing), network policies, secrets protection and supply-chain controls. Weakness in any layer can be exploited, so all must be configured.

first_principles.problem: A cluster with strong RBAC still allows privileged Pods that escape to the node.
truths: Each layer answers a different question.

analogy.title: Layers of airport security
analogy.story: ID checks, boarding passes, baggage screening and cabin rules.
analogy.breaks: Airports screen everyone the same way; Kubernetes layers must be configured per cluster.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No single layer carries all the weight.

check.q: Why isn't strong RBAC enough to secure a cluster?
check.a: It controls API actions but not what workloads do at runtime, such as privileged containers escaping to the node.

authentication-the-missing-user-database.core: Kubernetes has no user database. Humans authenticate via X.509 client certificates, OIDC tokens from an identity provider or webhook token authenticators; workloads use service account tokens (projected, short-lived, audience-bound). The API server extracts username and groups from the credential and passes them to authorisation.

first_principles.problem: Teams share an admin kubeconfig with a long-lived client certificate that can't be revoked.
truths: Corporate identity lives in an IdP.

analogy.title: A building that accepts an external ID card system
analogy.story: It doesn't keep its own staff list; it trusts badges issued by HR.
analogy.breaks: Badges are checked on entry; OIDC tokens expire and must be refreshed.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Users log in with corporate SSO; groups drive RBAC.

check.q: Why avoid client certificates for human users?
check.a: Kubernetes can't easily revoke them, and they're often long-lived.

identity-brokers-dex-and-keycloak.core: Identity brokers such as Dex and Keycloak sit between Kubernetes (and other tools) and upstream identity sources (LDAP, Active Directory, SAML, GitHub, Google), issuing standard OIDC tokens with group claims. This gives one login for clusters, dashboards and GitOps tools, even when upstream IdPs don't speak OIDC.

first_principles.problem: The company uses LDAP and SAML, but the Kubernetes API server only understands OIDC.
truths: Many tools benefit from one login.
derivation: Point **API server OIDC** at the broker.

analogy.title: A translator at a border crossing
analogy.story: Travellers arrive with documents in many languages; the translator issues a standard local pass.
analogy.breaks: Translators can be tricked; brokers must be highly available and secured since they gate all access.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: LDAP users log into Kubernetes with group claims.

code.text:
connectors:
- type: ldap
  id: corp-ldap
  name: Corporate LDAP
  config:
    host: ldap.corp.example.com:636
    userSearch: {baseDN: ou=people,dc=corp,dc=example,dc=com, username: uid, idAttr: uid, emailAttr: mail}
    groupSearch: {baseDN: ou=groups,dc=corp,dc=example,dc=com, userMatchers: [{userAttr: DN, groupAttr: member}], nameAttr: cn}

check.q: What problem do Dex and Keycloak solve for Kubernetes?
check.a: They translate identities from LDAP, SAML and other IdPs into OIDC tokens the API server accepts.

rbac-evaluation-logic.core: RBAC is additive and deny-by-default: Roles (namespaced) and ClusterRoles (cluster-wide or reusable) list allowed verbs on resources; RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings grant them to users, groups or service accounts. A request is allowed if any binding grants it, and there are no deny rules. Watch for escalation verbs (bind, escalate, impersonate) and wildcard permissions.

first_principles.problem: A developer is granted 'edit' cluster-wide and can read every namespace's Secrets.
derivation: Use **ClusterRoles** as reusable templates bound per namespace.
Audit with **kubectl auth can-i** and rbac-tools.

analogy.title: Keys on a keyring
analogy.story: You can open any door any of your keys fits; there's no 'anti-key'.
analogy.breaks: Keys are physical; RBAC permissions can be granted to whole groups at once.

check.q: Can RBAC express an explicit deny?
check.a: No; RBAC is purely additive and anything not granted is denied.

pod-security-the-evolution-from-psp-to-p.core: PodSecurityPolicy (removed in 1.25) was confusing: policies applied via RBAC 'use' permissions, and ordering and mutation surprised users. It was replaced by Pod Security Standards (three fixed profiles: privileged, baseline, restricted) enforced by the built-in Pod Security Admission controller via namespace labels, with richer custom policy left to Kyverno, Gatekeeper or CEL ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

first_principles.problem: Clusters upgraded past 1.25 lost PSP enforcement, and teams didn't replace it.
truths: Most clusters need the same few profiles.

analogy.title: Replacing a confusing rulebook with three clear dress codes
analogy.story: Casual, business and formal, applied per room.
analogy.breaks: Dress codes don't cover every situation; custom policy engines fill the gaps.

example.title: Migration path
flow: Map PSP rules to PSS levels

check.a: Pod Security Standards enforced by Pod Security Admission (plus policy engines for custom rules).

pod-security-standards-pss-levels.core: Privileged is unrestricted (for system components). Baseline blocks known privilege escalations: no privileged containers, host namespaces, hostPath, host ports or dangerous capabilities. Restricted adds hardening best practices: runAsNonRoot, drop ALL capabilities, no privilege escalation, seccomp RuntimeDefault and restricted volume types.

first_principles.problem: Teams don't know what 'secure enough' means for a Pod spec.
truths: Known escalation paths can be blocked.

analogy.title: Building safety ratings
analogy.story: Plant rooms (privileged), standard offices (baseline) and clean rooms (restricted).
analogy.breaks: Ratings rarely change; PSS versions evolve with Kubernetes releases.

check.q: Which PSS level requires runAsNonRoot and dropping all capabilities?

pod-security-admission-psa-modes.core: Pod Security Admission applies PSS levels per namespace via labels for three modes: enforce (reject violating Pods), audit (record violations in audit logs) and warn (return warnings to the user). Each mode can pin a version. Roll out by warning and auditing first, then enforcing, and exempt only specific users, runtime classes or namespaces when unavoidable.

first_principles.problem: Enforcing restricted immediately breaks dozens of existing deployments.
derivation: Configure **exemptions** sparingly in the admission config.

analogy.title: Introducing a new traffic rule
analogy.story: Warning notices first, then logging offenders, then issuing fines.
analogy.breaks: Drivers can contest fines; enforced PSA rejections are immediate.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Baseline enforced; restricted violations visible before enforcing.

code.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted

check.q: Which PSA mode returns warnings to kubectl users without blocking?
